title: Medium exam 10
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace a few steps: cut fields and characters, type and whereis, standard streams, absolute and relative paths, group permissions, suspending a job, root's environment, assignments, xargs with spaces and exit inside functions.

questions.title: Fields and characters
questions.text: The line is `root:x:0`. What do `cut -d: -f2` and `cut -c2` print for it, in that order?

options.t: `x` and `o`
options.why: `-f2` takes the second field using `:` as the separator; `-c2` takes the second character of the line.

options.t: `x` and `x`
options.why: The second character of `root:x:0` is `o`; the `x` is the sixth.

options.t: `o` and `x`
options.why: The options are swapped: `-f` selects fields and `-c` selects characters.

options.t: `root:x` and `ro`
options.why: `-f2` and `-c2` select a single field and a single character, not a range.

questions.title: Finding commands
questions.text: Which statement about `type`, `which` and `whereis` is FALSE?

options.t: `type cd` reports that `cd` is a shell builtin.
options.why: True: it prints `cd is a shell builtin`.

options.t: `which ls` prints the path of the program that would run when you type `ls`.
options.why: True: for example `/usr/bin/ls`.

options.t: `type` also reports aliases and functions, which the others do not know about.
options.why: True: it asks the shell itself how it would interpret the word.

options.t: `whereis ls` only looks in the `PATH` and prints just the executable.
options.why: False: `whereis` also looks for the manual pages and the sources, and prints them with the binary.

questions.title: What > captures
questions.text: Which statement about `ls /nonexistent /etc/hostname > out.txt` is FALSE?

options.t: `/etc/hostname` is written into `out.txt`.
options.why: True: the standard output goes to the file.

options.t: The error message about `/nonexistent` appears on the screen.
options.why: True: `>` redirects only the stream 1.

options.t: `out.txt` is created even if the command prints nothing on stdout.
options.why: True: the shell creates (or truncates) the file before running the command.

options.t: The error message about `/nonexistent` is also written into `out.txt`.
options.why: False: the standard error is a different stream; it would need `2>&1` or `2> file`.

questions.title: cd with a leading slash
questions.text: You are in `/home/ana` and both `/home/ana/docs` and `/docs` exist. Compare `cd docs` and `cd /docs`.

options.t: `cd docs` goes to `/home/ana/docs`; `cd /docs` goes to `/docs`.
options.why: A path without a leading `/` starts at the current directory; one with it starts at the root.

options.t: Both go to `/home/ana/docs`, because `cd` always starts in the home directory.
options.why: Only `cd` with no argument goes to the home directory.

options.t: `cd docs` goes to `/docs` and `cd /docs` goes to `/home/ana/docs`.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.t: Both go to `/docs`, because the leading slash is optional.
options.why: Without the slash the path is relative to the current directory.

questions.title: What the group can do
questions.text: `prog` belongs to the user `ana` and the group `devs`, with mode `-rwxr-x---`. `bob` is a member of `devs`. What can `bob` do with `prog`?

options.t: Read it and run it, but not modify it.
options.why: `bob` is not the owner, so the group bits `r-x` apply to him.

options.t: Read, modify and run it, because he belongs to the group.
options.why: The group has no write permission: its bits are `r-x`.

options.t: Nothing, because only the owner can use the file.
options.why: The group bits give read and execute permission to the members of `devs`.

options.t: Only run it, because reading is a permission of the owner.
options.why: The group has `r` as well.

questions.title: Pausing a long job
questions.text: A long `sort` is running in the foreground. You need the prompt for a moment, but you must not lose the work of the `sort`. Which sequence does it?

options.t: `Ctrl+Z`, type your commands, then `fg`
options.why: `Ctrl+Z` suspends the job without ending it, and `fg` brings it back.

options.t: `Ctrl+C`, type your commands, then `fg`
options.why: `Ctrl+C` terminates the `sort`, so there is nothing left to bring back.

options.t: `Ctrl+D`, type your commands, then `fg`
options.why: `Ctrl+D` sends end-of-file to the input; it does not give the prompt back.

options.t: `Ctrl+Z`, then `kill %1` to free the terminal.
options.why: `kill %1` ends the job, and its work is lost.

questions.title: The environment of root
questions.text: Logged in as `root` with a normal login, you run `whoami; id -u; echo $HOME`. What is printed?

options.t: `root`, `0` and `/root`
options.why: root is the administrator account: UID 0, and its home directory is `/root`, outside `/home`.

options.t: `root`, `0` and `/home/root`
options.why: root's home directory is not under `/home`.

options.t: `root`, `1` and `/root`
options.why: UID 1 belongs to `daemon`; root has UID 0.

options.t: `admin`, `0` and `/root`
options.why: The account is called `root`, not `admin`.

options.t: `file=report.txt`
options.why: An assignment has no spaces around `=`, and `${file}` is followed by the text `_old`.

options.t: `file = report.txt`
options.why: With spaces it is the command `file` with two arguments (`=` and `report.txt`).

options.t: `$file=report.txt`
options.why: A `$` on the left expands the variable: the shell tries to run a command called `=report.txt`.

options.t: `file report.txt`
options.why: It runs the command `file`, which describes the type of `report.txt`; no variable is set.

questions.title: xargs and file names with spaces
questions.text: `my notes.txt` (two lines) and `c.txt` (empty) exist. What does `find . -name '*.txt' | xargs wc -l` do?

options.t: It reports errors for `./my` and `notes.txt`, because `xargs` splits the name at the space.
options.why: By default `xargs` splits its input on whitespace; `-print0` with `xargs -0` avoids the problem.

options.t: It prints the line counts of both files correctly.
options.why: The name with a space is split into two words.

options.t: It prints only the counts of the files without spaces and silently skips the other.
options.why: `wc` receives the two pieces and complains about each.

options.t: It fails before running anything, because `find` cannot output names with spaces.
options.why: `find` prints them normally; the problem appears in `xargs`.

questions.title: exit inside a function
questions.text: A script runs `f() { exit 3; }`, then `f`, then `echo after`. What happens?

options.t: The script ends with status 3 when `f` is called, and `after` is never printed.
options.why: `exit` ends the shell that executes it, even inside a function; `return` is what leaves only the function.

options.t: `after` is printed and the status of the script is 3.
options.why: `echo` is never reached.

options.t: `after` is printed and the status of the script is 0.
options.why: The script has already ended.

options.t: The script prints an error, because `exit` cannot be used inside a function.
options.why: It can be used; it just ends the whole script.
